giza.name: Pyramids of Giza
giza.description: The tombs of the pharaohs Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure of Egypt's Fourth Dynasty, and the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that survives largely intact.
facts: The Great Pyramid of Khufu originally stood about 146 meters high and was the tallest man-made structure in the world for nearly four thousand years.
About 2.3 million blocks of limestone and granite were used.
The four sides are aligned almost exactly with the four cardinal directions.
The Great Sphinx in front is about 73 meters long and was carved from a single mass of limestone bedrock.

detail.overview: The Giza pyramid complex stands on the Giza Plateau southwest of Cairo and is a group of funerary monuments built by the Fourth Dynasty pharaohs Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure across three generations. The ancient Egyptians believed that after death a pharaoh ascended to the heavens and became a god, and the pyramids were colossal monuments that protected the body and helped the pharaoh's spirit pass into the afterlife. Besides the three great pyramids, the complex includes queens' pyramids, mortuary temples, valley temples, causeways and the Great Sphinx. Of these, the Pyramid of Khufu is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and the only one that has survived largely intact to the present day.

Base of the Pyramid of Khufu
stats.value: About 230.3 m per side, covering about 5.3 hectares

stats.label: Number of blocks
stats.value: About 2.3 million for the Pyramid of Khufu

stats.value: Pharaonic tomb and royal funerary complex

history.text: The Pyramid of Khufu is largely completed; the work is believed to have been directed by the vizier Hemiunu.
Khafre builds the second pyramid alongside; the Sphinx is generally believed to have been built during his reign as well.
The Pyramid of Menkaure is built, noticeably smaller than the first two.
Thutmose IV clears away the sand burying the Sphinx and sets up the "Dream Stele."
The Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun has a passage cut into the north face of the Pyramid of Khufu to enter its interior.
The spire of Lincoln Cathedral in England is completed, and the Pyramid of Khufu finally loses its title as the world's tallest structure, held for about 3,800 years.
Archaeologists discover a sealed boat pit on the south side of the Pyramid of Khufu, yielding the intact cedar "Khufu ship."
The international ScanPyramids project, using cosmic-ray muon imaging, detects a large void above the Grand Gallery.
The Grand Egyptian Museum opens fully beside the Giza Plateau, and the Khufu ship and other artifacts are moved there for display.

parts.name: Pyramid of Khufu
parts.description: The largest of the three, also called the Great Pyramid; inside are the King's Chamber, the Queen's Chamber, a subterranean chamber and the Grand Gallery, about 8.6 meters high.

parts.name: Pyramid of Khafre
parts.description: Originally about 143.5 meters high; because it stands on higher ground it looks taller than the Pyramid of Khufu, and part of its original limestone casing still remains at the top.

parts.name: Pyramid of Menkaure
parts.description: Originally about 65 meters high, the smallest of the three; its lower casing used red granite.

parts.name: Queens' pyramids
parts.description: Beside each of the three great pyramids stand several small subsidiary pyramids, where queens or royal women were buried.

parts.name: The Great Sphinx
parts.description: About 73 meters long and 20 meters high, carved from the limestone bedrock in place; its face is generally believed to be that of Khafre.

parts.name: Valley temples and causeways
parts.description: The valley temple stands near the Nile floodplain and was the starting point of the burial rites, linked by a causeway to the mortuary temple beside the pyramid.

parts.name: Boat pits
parts.description: Boat-shaped pits dug around the pyramids that held solar barques for the pharaoh's voyage in the afterlife; the Khufu ship is about 43 meters long.

detail.architecture: The pyramids were built by stacking courses of locally quarried limestone, while key parts such as the burial chambers used granite brought from Aswan about 800 kilometers away. The exterior was originally covered with polished white Tura limestone, making the whole pyramid gleam in the sunlight, but most of the casing was stripped in the Middle Ages to build Cairo. The sides of the Pyramid of Khufu deviate only slightly from true north, south, east and west, and above the King's Chamber are five relieving chambers that spread the weight of the massive stones above.
detail.visit: The Giza pyramids are open to visitors today; an additional ticket allows entry into the Pyramid of Khufu, and there is a sound-and-light show at night. The nearby Grand Egyptian Museum houses a large collection of artifacts from the pharaonic era and is well worth combining with a visit to the pyramids.

stonehenge.name: Stonehenge
stonehenge.description: A ring-shaped monument enclosed by huge standing stones, aligned with the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset; its purpose may have been connected with ritual, calendar-keeping and burial.
facts: Some of the "bluestones" came from the Preseli Hills in Wales, about 240 kilometers away.
The largest sarsen stones weigh about 25 tonnes.
Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.

detail.overview: Stonehenge stands on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, southern England, and is the best-known prehistoric stone monument in Europe. It was built in stages by people from the Neolithic to the Bronze Age over some fifteen hundred years. The main axis of the stones is aligned with the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset, and scholars believe it may have served as a place of ritual, calendar-keeping, burial and assembly; large quantities of cremated remains have been excavated at the site. Its builders had neither metal tools nor wheels, yet they moved and raised stones weighing dozens of tonnes, which still amazes people today.

stats.label: Builders
stats.value: Inhabitants of Britain from the Neolithic to the Bronze Age

stats.label: Tallest stone
stats.value: Uprights of the Great Trilithon, about 7.3 m high (the part above ground)

stats.label: Weight of the stones
stats.value: Large sarsen stones of about 25 tonnes

history.text: A circular ditch and bank are dug, forming the earliest "enclosure," with 56 Aubrey Holes on the inner side.
Some bluestones may have arrived at the site, and the site begins to be used as a cremation cemetery.
The large sarsen stones are raised, forming the outer sarsen circle and the five trilithons arranged in a horseshoe inside.
The bluestones are rearranged several times, and in the final phase the Y and Z holes are dug on the outside.
Local man Cecil Chubb buys Stonehenge at auction for £6,600.
Chubb donates Stonehenge to the British government, which takes responsibility for protecting it.
Inscribed as a World Heritage Site together with the nearby Avebury stone circle.
A new visitor center opens about 2.4 kilometers from the stones, and the old car park and road are returned to grass.
Research confirms that the central "Altar Stone" came from northeastern Scotland, about 700 kilometers away.

parts.name: Sarsen circle
parts.description: Originally a continuous ring of 30 upright sarsen stones topped by 30 lintels, the lintels joined by mortise-and-tenon and tongue-and-groove joints.

parts.name: Trilithons
parts.description: Five huge gateways in the inner circle, each made of two uprights carrying one horizontal stone, arranged in a horseshoe open to the northeast.

parts.name: Bluestone circle and bluestone horseshoe
parts.description: The smaller bluestones came from the Preseli Hills in Wales and were arranged inside the sarsen circle and the trilithons.

parts.name: Altar Stone
parts.description: A large sandstone slab lying at the center; a 2024 study showed it came from northeastern Scotland.

parts.name: Heel Stone
parts.description: A natural boulder standing outside the entrance; at midsummer, viewed from the center, the sun rises near it.

parts.name: Ditch and bank
parts.description: The earliest circular earthwork, whose 56 Aubrey Holes on the inner side have yielded cremated remains.

parts.name: The Avenue
parts.description: An ancient track flanked by two parallel banks, running about 2.8 kilometers from the northeast entrance to the River Avon.

detail.architecture: The sarsen stones of Stonehenge were pounded and dressed into shape; mortise holes were cut in the underside of the lintels to fit over tenons on the tops of the uprights, and the lintels were joined to one another with tongue-and-groove joints, a rare example of carpentry techniques applied to stone. The tops of the uprights are slightly narrower and the lintels slightly curved to follow the circle, and the uprights bulge a little at mid-height, perhaps to correct the visual effect when seen from below. Scholars suppose that the stones were hauled with sledges, rollers or tracks and a great deal of manpower.
detail.visit: Stonehenge is managed by English Heritage. Visitors usually view it from the path around the outside of the stone circle, and the visitor center has exhibitions and reconstructed Neolithic houses. At the summer and winter solstices the public is allowed inside the circle to watch the sunrise or sunset.

parthenon.name: The Parthenon
parthenon.description: A temple dedicated to Athena, patron goddess of Athens, built in the age of Pericles; a symbol of classical Greek architecture and of the golden age of democratic Athens.
facts: The columns lean slightly inward and swell at mid-height (entasis) to correct optical illusions.
In 1687, when Venetian forces bombarded it, gunpowder stored inside exploded, severely damaging the building.
Some of the sculptures are now in the British Museum in London, and the dispute over their return continues to this day.

detail.overview: The Parthenon stands at the highest point of the Acropolis of Athens and is a temple dedicated to Athena Parthenos ("Athena the Virgin"), the city's patron goddess. After Athens defeated Persia and became leader of the Delian League, it was built under the direction of the statesman Pericles; the architects were Ictinus and Callicrates, and the sculpture was overseen by Phidias. Built of Pentelic marble and employing many refined optical corrections, it is regarded as the supreme achievement of the Doric order. It has served as a church, a mosque and a powder magazine, and remains a symbol of classical Greek civilization and Western democracy.

stats.label: Commissioned by
stats.value: The city-state of Athens under Pericles

stats.label: Columns
stats.value: 46 columns in the outer colonnade (8 × 17), each about 10.4 m high

history.text: The Persian army captures Athens and burns the "Pre-Parthenon," then under construction on the Acropolis.
Pericles launches the rebuilding of the Acropolis, and work begins on the Parthenon.
The main structure of the temple is completed, and Phidias's chryselephantine statue of Athena is dedicated.
The decorative work, including the pediment sculptures, is finished.
The temple is converted into a Christian church dedicated to the Virgin Mary.
After the Ottoman Empire takes Athens, the temple is converted into a mosque and a minaret is added.
Venetian forces bombard the Acropolis; the gunpowder stored inside explodes, and the roof and long stretches of wall and columns collapse.
Agents of the British Lord Elgin remove large numbers of sculptures, which are later sold to the British Museum.
Greece establishes the Committee for the Conservation of the Acropolis Monuments and begins restoration work that continues to this day.

parts.name: Peristyle colonnade
parts.description: The 46 Doric columns surrounding the temple, 8 on the front and 17 on the sides.

parts.name: Metopes
parts.description: A total of 92 square relief panels on the frieze above the columns depict mythological battles such as gods versus giants and Greeks versus Amazons.

parts.name: Ionic frieze
parts.description: A continuous relief about 160 meters long running around the top of the outer wall of the cella, depicting the procession of the Panathenaic festival.

parts.name: East and west pediments
parts.description: The east pediment carves the birth of Athena from the head of Zeus, and the west pediment depicts the contest between Athena and Poseidon for the patronage of Athens.

parts.name: Cella
parts.description: The main hall of the temple, which originally housed Phidias's chryselephantine statue of Athena, about 12 meters high.

parts.name: Opisthodomos (rear chamber)
parts.description: A room on the west side supported by four Ionic columns, used as a treasury for the funds of the city and the Delian League.

detail.architecture: The Parthenon has hardly a single true straight line: the center of the platform rises slightly, the columns lean a little inward, the shafts swell at mid-height (entasis), and the corner columns are thickened and set closer together, to counteract the illusions of sagging and thinning seen by the human eye. The marble blocks are joined without mortar, using iron I-shaped clamps and dowels, then lead poured around them to prevent rust. The whole temple was designed with precise proportional relationships, and many dimensions show a ratio of about 4:9.
detail.visit: The Parthenon stands within the Acropolis site in Athens; visitors may view it from around the outside but cannot enter, and restoration scaffolding is often seen on the building. The Acropolis Museum at the foot of the hill opened in 2009, and its top floor displays the Parthenon frieze in its actual orientation.

great-wall.name: The Great Wall of China
great-wall.description: Defensive works built by successive dynasties to resist the nomadic peoples of the north; after the unification under the First Emperor of Qin, the walls of the former states were linked, and what is seen today is mostly Ming-era reconstruction.
facts: In 2012 the Chinese authorities announced that the total length of the Great Walls of all dynasties was about 21,196 kilometers.
That "the Great Wall is visible to the naked eye from space" is a common misconception.
Beacon towers were set along the line to relay military intelligence quickly by smoke and fire.

detail.overview: The Great Wall is a defensive system built by successive Chinese dynasties to resist the nomadic peoples of the north. From the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods each state built its own walls, and after the unification under the First Emperor of Qin they were linked and extended. The best-known and best-preserved sections today are those of the Ming dynasty, which, after the Tumu Crisis, rebuilt the wall on a large scale in brick and stone, from Hushan in Liaoning in the east to Jiayuguan in Gansu in the west. The Ming sections in Beijing, such as Badaling, Mutianyu and Juyongguan, guard the routes to the capital and are the most solidly built and most densely garrisoned stretches of the Wall. The Great Wall is not merely a wall but a complete military system made up of walls, passes, watchtowers, beacon towers and garrison forts.

stats.label: Date of construction
stats.value: Built by successive dynasties from the 7th century BC; the Beijing sections are mainly Ming (1368–1644)

stats.label: Principal builders
stats.value: Successive Ming emperors, with generals such as Xu Da and Qi Jiguang directing the work

stats.label: Total length of the Ming Wall
Total length of the Walls of all dynasties
Dimensions of the Badaling wall
stats.value: Average height about 7.8 m, width at the top about 5.8 m

stats.label: Main materials
stats.value: Wall bricks, stone slabs and rammed earth, bonded with lime (in places mixed with sticky-rice paste)

stats.label: Purpose
stats.value: Military defense, garrisoning, signaling by beacon, and control of trade at the passes

history.text: The state of Chu builds the "Fangcheng" wall in the Spring and Autumn period, and in the Warring States period the other states also build walls to protect themselves.
The First Emperor of Qin sends Meng Tian north against the Xiongnu, linking and extending the old walls of Qin, Zhao and Yan, known as the "Ten-Thousand-Li Great Wall."
The Ming dynasty is founded, and the general Xu Da begins building passes and border walls in the north; Juyongguan and other fortified passes are built one after another.
In the Tumu Crisis the Ming emperor Yingzong is captured by the Oirats, and afterward the Ming greatly strengthens the Great Wall defenses.
The Badaling pass is completed, guarding the northern mouth of Juyongguan and becoming an important bulwark northwest of Beijing.
Qi Jiguang, as commander of Jizhen, builds more than a thousand hollow watchtowers in the Beijing and Hebei area and faces the walls with brick and stone.
Wu Sangui opens Shanhaiguan to let the Qing army through, after which the Great Wall gradually loses its military function.
The "Love China, Restore the Great Wall" public sponsorship campaign begins, and sections such as Badaling and Mutianyu are restored one after another.
The Great Wall is inscribed as a World Heritage Site.

parts.name: Wall body
parts.description: In the Beijing sections the wall is mostly built on a base of stone slabs, faced with wall bricks on the outside and filled with earth and stone inside, rising and falling along the ridgelines.

parts.name: Crenellations and parapet
parts.description: On the outer side of the wall top is a crenellated wall with loopholes, and on the inner side a lower parapet to keep soldiers from falling.

parts.name: Watchtowers
parts.description: Towers rising above the wall; hollow watchtowers could garrison troops and store weapons and fire out through arrow windows.

parts.name: Beacon towers
parts.description: Free-standing platforms built on commanding heights, lighting smoke by day and fire by night to relay news of the enemy.

parts.name: Fortified passes
parts.description: Such as Juyongguan and Badaling, heavily garrisoned fortified towns on main routes, with gates controlling the passage of people and merchants.

parts.name: Walkways and access points
parts.description: The passage along the top of the wall allowed soldiers and horses to be moved, and access points connect to the inner side of the wall by steps or ramps.

parts.name: Forts and garrison posts
parts.description: Garrison forts along the wall housed troops and supplies, forming the defense in depth of the "Nine Frontier Garrisons."

detail.architecture: The Ming Great Wall followed the principle of "following the terrain and using natural barriers to build defenses," mostly running along ridgelines so that the steep mountains themselves served as barriers. In the Beijing sections the wall is generally built on a base of granite slabs, faced above with large fired wall bricks bonded with lime mortar; some studies have confirmed that sticky-rice paste was mixed into the mortar to increase adhesion and durability. At steep places the wall slope can exceed 70 degrees and the wall top becomes a staircase, with watchtowers spaced from several tens to several hundred meters apart so they can support one another.
detail.visit: In Beijing, sections such as Badaling, Mutianyu, Juyongguan and Simatai have been restored and opened, some with cable cars or toboggan slides, and they are crowded with visitors in peak season. Unrestored "wild wall" sections such as Jiankou are steep and mostly closed to climbing, so visitors should choose the open scenic areas.

chichen-itza.name: Chichen Itza · Temple of Kukulcan
chichen-itza.description: The central building of the ancient Maya city of Chichen Itza, a stepped pyramid and also a giant calendar in stone.
facts: Each of the four stairways has 91 steps, which with the platform at the top make 365, matching the days of the year.
At the spring and autumn equinoxes, sunlight casts a shadow on the side of the stairway like a feathered serpent winding down.
Clapping in front of the pyramid produces an echo that sounds like the call of a quetzal.

detail.overview: Chichen Itza is one of the most important Maya cities on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, reaching its height from about the 9th to the 12th century, with an architectural style blending Maya and central Mexican Toltec cultures. The Pyramid of Kukulcan at the center of the city (called "El Castillo," meaning "the castle," by the Spanish) is dedicated to the feathered serpent god Kukulcan. The number of steps, platforms and divisions of the pyramid all correspond to the Maya calendar, and the play of light and shadow at the spring and autumn equinoxes, like a feathered serpent crawling down the stairway, shows the Maya's precise astronomical knowledge. Chichen Itza was chosen in 2007 as one of the "New Seven Wonders of the World."

stats.label: Date of construction
stats.value: c. 9th–12th century (outer layer of the pyramid c. 10th–12th century)

stats.label: Builders
stats.value: The Maya (Itza people), influenced by Toltec culture

stats.label: Height
stats.value: About 30 m (including the temple at the top, about 6 m)

stats.label: Base
stats.value: A square about 55.3 m on each side

stats.label: Stairways
stats.value: 91 steps on each of the four sides, 365 with the top platform

history.text: A settlement begins to form around Chichen Itza, near the natural wells (cenotes) that provided water.
The city expands rapidly, becoming the political and religious center of northern Yucatán, and the early inner pyramid is built.
The outer Pyramid of Kukulcan is built enclosing the older pyramid, and the Temple of the Warriors and the Great Ball Court are built in the same period.
Chichen Itza declines and the political center shifts to Mayapan, but the sacred cenote remains a place of pilgrimage.
The Spanish conquistador Francisco de Montejo the Younger briefly occupies Chichen Itza before being driven out by the Maya.
Archaeologists discover an earlier inner pyramid inside the pyramid, containing a red jaguar throne and a Chac Mool statue.
The ancient city of Chichen Itza is inscribed as a World Heritage Site.
To protect the monument and for visitor safety, climbing the pyramid is prohibited.
Chosen as one of the "New Seven Wonders of the World."

parts.name: Nine terraces
parts.description: The pyramid is made of nine progressively receding platforms stacked up, with each face divided in half by the stairway, making 18 sections in all, corresponding to the 18 months of the Maya calendar.

parts.name: Four stairways
parts.description: 91 steps on each of the four sides, 365 with the top platform, matching the days of the year.

parts.name: Feathered serpent head carvings
parts.description: At the foot of the north stairway, huge feathered serpent heads are carved on both sides, where the head of the "light-and-shadow serpent" of the equinoxes is found.

parts.name: Temple at the top
parts.description: A temple about 6 meters high at the summit of the pyramid, with its main entrance facing north and supported by columns in the form of feathered serpents.

parts.name: Inner pyramid
parts.description: An earlier pyramid enclosed by the outer one, with nine terraces and a single north-facing stairway, containing a jaguar throne and a Chac Mool figure.

parts.name: Sacred Cenote
parts.description: A natural limestone sinkhole about 300 meters north of the pyramid, linked to it by a stone-paved causeway, into which offerings and human sacrifices were thrown.

detail.architecture: The Pyramid of Kukulcan is built of limestone using the "nesting" technique of enclosing a new building directly around an older one, so an earlier pyramid is preserved inside. The four stairways are aligned precisely with the cardinal directions, and on the afternoons of the equinoxes the corners of the terraces at the northwest cast seven triangles of light and shadow on the balustrade of the north stairway, joining the serpent's head at the bottom to form a feathered serpent. When one claps in front of the pyramid, the steps produce an echo like the call of a quetzal, which scholars suppose may be related to the periodic structure of the steps.
detail.visit: The Chichen Itza archaeological zone is open to visitors; climbing the pyramid is now prohibited, but visitors can view it up close and watch the light-and-shadow serpent phenomenon around the spring and autumn equinoxes. The site is in the state of Yucatán, and day trips from Cancún or Mérida are common.

colosseum.name: The Colosseum
colosseum.description: A huge elliptical amphitheater built by the Flavian dynasty and used for gladiatorial combats, wild-animal shows and public festivals; a representative work of ancient Roman engineering.
facts: It is estimated to have held about 50,000 to 80,000 spectators.
Beneath it are complex passages and lifting mechanisms that let wild animals suddenly appear on the arena floor.
Roman concrete and arch construction were used extensively.

detail.overview: The Colosseum's formal name is the Flavian Amphitheater. It was ordered built by the Flavian emperor Vespasian on the site of the artificial lake of Emperor Nero's "Golden House," symbolizing the return of the land to the Roman people. It was inaugurated by his son Titus in AD 80 with games lasting 100 days, and Domitian later added the underground structures. The arena was used for gladiator fights, wild-beast hunts, executions and mythological dramas, and was the largest amphitheater of the ancient world. Even though much of its outer wall is ruined, it remains a symbol of the engineering skill and power of the Roman Empire.

stats.label: Dimensions
stats.value: Major axis about 189 m, minor axis about 156 m

stats.label: Main materials
stats.value: Travertine, tuff, brick and Roman concrete

history.text: Vespasian orders an amphitheater built on the site of the artificial lake of Nero's Golden House.
Emperor Titus presides over the inauguration and holds games lasting 100 days.
During Domitian's reign the underground passages and mechanisms (the hypogeum) are added and the top-level seating is completed.
A lightning strike starts a great fire that burns the wooden structure of the upper levels, and repairs continue for decades.
The last gladiatorial contest recorded in the sources; wild-beast shows continue into the early 6th century.
A great earthquake brings down the south outer wall, and the fallen stone is later carried off to build churches and palaces.
Pope Benedict XIV consecrates the Colosseum to the Passion of Christ, regarding it as a place sacred to the martyrs, and forbids further removal of stone.
Chosen as one of the "New Seven Wonders of the World."
A large-scale cleaning and restoration of the outer wall is carried out, washing away centuries of grime.

parts.name: Outer facade
parts.description: About 48 meters high; the lower three levels are arcades, using Doric (Tuscan), Ionic and Corinthian half-columns from bottom to top.

parts.name: Seating
parts.description: Divided by social class: senators sat in the front rows nearest the arena, while women and commoners mostly sat on the uppermost level.

parts.name: Arena floor
parts.description: Originally laid with a wooden floor covered with sand to absorb blood; the Latin word for "sand" is the origin of the word arena.

parts.name: Hypogeum (underground chambers)
parts.description: Two levels of passages and rooms beneath the arena floor, used to hold wild animals and gladiators and to raise them to the arena by hand-operated winch lifts.

parts.name: Entrances and passages
parts.description: The ground floor has 80 arched entrances, of which 76 were for spectators and numbered, allowing crowds to disperse quickly.

parts.name: Awning
parts.description: Brackets and masts on the top-level wall allowed a canvas awning to be spread for shade, operated by sailors of the Roman navy.

detail.architecture: The Colosseum's outer walls and main piers are of travertine, supported inside by tuff, brick and Roman concrete; the travertine alone is estimated to have required about 100,000 cubic meters. The structure uses rings of radiating arches and barrel vaults to support the seating tier by tier, both distributing weight and forming ring corridors and stairways. The stone blocks were originally held together with iron clamps; in the Middle Ages people dug out the metal, leaving the many holes seen in the outer wall today.
detail.visit: The Colosseum today forms part of the Colosseum Archaeological Park, sharing a ticket with the Roman Forum and the Palatine Hill; advance online booking is recommended. Special guided-tour tickets allow entry to the hypogeum and the top level.

angkor-wat.name: Angkor Wat
angkor-wat.description: Built by the Khmer Empire king Suryavarman II, originally dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu and later converted into a Buddhist temple; one of the largest religious complexes in the world.
facts: Five lotus-bud towers symbolize Mount Meru, the center of the universe.
Relief carvings in the galleries depict scenes from the Indian epics, such as the "Churning of the Ocean of Milk."
The image of Angkor Wat appears on the flag of Cambodia.

detail.overview: Angkor Wat stands north of Siem Reap in Cambodia. It is the state temple built in the first half of the 12th century by the Khmer Empire king Suryavarman II, originally dedicated to the chief Hindu god Vishnu and possibly also the king's funerary temple. The whole temple takes the cosmology of Mount Meru as its blueprint: the five lotus-bud towers at the center symbolize the five peaks of Mount Meru, and the broad moat around the outside represents the ocean encircling the world. Unlike most Khmer temples, Angkor Wat faces west rather than east, and its galleries are covered with exquisite reliefs. After the 13th century it gradually became a Theravada Buddhist temple, and monks are still active there today; it is one of the largest religious complexes in the world.

stats.label: Outer extent
stats.value: About 1.5 × 1.3 km, with a moat about 190 m wide

history.text: Suryavarman II takes the throne and soon begins building Angkor Wat, dedicated to Vishnu.
The king dies and the main body of the temple is largely complete, though some reliefs remain unfinished.
Cham forces capture Angkor; Jayavarman VII later retakes it and builds a new city, Angkor Thom.
Theravada Buddhism spreads in the Khmer lands, and Angkor Wat gradually becomes a Buddhist temple.
The Siamese kingdom of Ayutthaya captures Angkor and the Khmer court later moves south, but monks continue to look after Angkor Wat.
The Portuguese friar António da Madalena visits, one of the first Europeans to record Angkor Wat.
The French naturalist Henri Mouhot visits and publishes a travel account, bringing Angkor Wat great fame in the West.
The École française d'Extrême-Orient begins the systematic clearing and restoration of the Angkor monuments.
The Angkor site is inscribed as a World Heritage Site and at the same time on the List in Danger; it is removed from the danger list in 2004.

parts.name: Moat
parts.description: A rectangular waterway about 190 meters wide surrounding the temple, symbolizing the cosmic ocean around Mount Meru.

parts.name: West causeway
parts.description: A stone causeway and approach crossing the moat, whose balustrades on both sides are carved with seven-headed nagas.

parts.name: Outer wall and entrance gopura
parts.description: The main west gopura is about 235 meters wide and is the principal entrance by which visitors enter the temple.

parts.name: Relief galleries
parts.description: The outer wall of the first-level gallery is about 800 meters long in all, carved with scenes such as the "Churning of the Ocean of Milk," the Ramayana, and heaven and hell.

parts.name: Cruciform gallery
parts.description: A cross-shaped gallery connecting the first and second levels, with square pools inside; on the wall is an ink inscription by the Japanese Morimoto Ukon Dayu dated 1632.

parts.name: Apsara reliefs
parts.description: More than a thousand celestial maidens (apsaras) with differing hairstyles and costumes are carved in the temple, representative of Khmer sculpture.

parts.name: Five central towers
parts.description: Five lotus-bud towers on the uppermost terrace, arranged in a quincunx, symbolizing the five peaks of Mount Meru, with the central tower the tallest.

detail.architecture: Angkor Wat consists of three square gallery terraces rising level by level, with the central tower at its core, forming a typical "temple-mountain." The walls and carvings use sandstone quarried from Mount Kulen about 40 kilometers away and transported by canals and waterways, while the foundations and inner structure mostly use coarser laterite. Almost no mortar is used between the blocks, which are held together by finely ground joints and tenons; the vaults use corbelling rather than true arches, so the gallery spaces are narrow and long.
detail.visit: Angkor Wat belongs to the Angkor Archaeological Park, and a one-day, three-day or seven-day pass must be purchased; it is about a 20-minute drive from central Siem Reap. Watching the reflection of the towers from the west pool at sunrise is the most popular sight, and the central tower on the uppermost level has dress-code rules and is open for limited times and numbers.

himeji.name: Himeji Castle
himeji.description: Nicknamed "White Heron Castle" because its white walls resemble a heron spreading its wings, it is one of the most complete surviving old castles in Japan, having escaped both war and earthquakes.
facts: In 1993 it became one of Japan's first World Heritage Sites, together with Hōryū-ji.
The maze-like passages inside the castle were designed to confuse invaders.
During the air raids of World War II an incendiary bomb landed on the keep but did not explode.

detail.overview: Himeji Castle stands on Mount Himeyama in Himeji, Hyōgo Prefecture, and is the largest and best-preserved early-modern castle in Japan. The keep complex seen today was largely rebuilt between 1601 and 1609 by Ikeda Terumasa, son-in-law of Tokugawa Ieyasu, and its white plaster walls look like a heron spreading its wings, hence the nickname "White Heron Castle." Inside, the main keep and three smaller keeps are linked by connecting corridor-turrets, forming a "linked keep" complex, with maze-like passages and various defensive features. Himeji Castle never experienced real combat, and also escaped the abolition of castles in the Meiji era, the air raids of World War II and the Great Hanshin Earthquake; in 1993 it became one of Japan's first World Heritage Sites together with Hōryū-ji.

stats.label: Main builders
stats.value: Built by the Akamatsu clan, enlarged by Hashiba (Toyotomi) Hideyoshi, keep complex rebuilt by Ikeda Terumasa

stats.label: Height of the main keep
stats.value: Keep itself about 31.5 m, about 46.4 m including the stone base

stats.label: Structure of the main keep
stats.value: Five stories externally, six floors internally plus one basement floor

stats.label: Main materials
stats.value: Timber frame, white plaster, tiles, stone walls

stats.label: Cultural properties
stats.value: 8 structures designated National Treasures, 74 designated Important Cultural Properties

history.text: Akamatsu Sadanori builds a castle on Mount Himeyama, generally regarded as the origin of Himeji Castle (according to tradition his father Akamatsu Norimura had already set up a fort here in 1333).
Hashiba Hideyoshi obtains Himeji Castle, rebuilds it as a stone-walled castle and builds a three-story keep as a base for the conquest of the Chūgoku region.
Ikeda Terumasa, enfeoffed after the Battle of Sekigahara, rebuilds the castle on a large scale, completing the five-story main keep and the linked-keep complex seen today.
Honda Tadamasa enters the castle and later builds the West Bailey for his son Tadatoki and Princess Sen.
During the Meiji government's abolition of castles, Himeji Castle is said to have been put up for auction at 23 yen 50 sen, and was preserved because the cost of demolition was too high.
The keep complex of Himeji Castle is designated a (former) National Treasure.
U.S. air raids burn the city of Himeji; an incendiary bomb that landed on the keep did not explode, and the castle was spared.
The "Shōwa Great Restoration" completely dismantles and reassembles the main keep and replaces the rotted central pillar.
The "Heisei Great Restoration" repaints the white plaster and replaces the roof tiles, and the main keep reopens in March 2015.

parts.name: Main keep
parts.description: Five stories externally and six floors internally plus one basement floor, supported by two huge central pillars running through all the levels, east and west.

parts.name: Smaller keeps
parts.description: Three three-story smaller keeps (East, Inui and West), which with the main keep enclose a rectangular courtyard.

parts.name: Connecting turrets
parts.description: Two-story turrets joining the main keep to the smaller keeps, so that the keep complex forms a "linked keep" that can give mutual support.

parts.name: Hishi Gate
parts.description: The first gate on entering the castle and the largest surviving gate, with ornate flame-shaped windows on the gate.

parts.name: West Bailey and Keshō Turret
parts.description: The area built for Princess Sen, linked by the long Hyakken Corridor; the Keshō Turret is said to be where Princess Sen did her toilette and rested.

parts.name: Loopholes and stone-drop openings
parts.description: The walls have round, triangular and square loopholes (sama), as well as stone-drop openings (ishiotoshi) from which stones could be dropped or shots fired downward.

parts.name: Stone walls
parts.description: Stone walls that curve upward in a fan-shaped taper, containing masonry from different periods, with some stones even taken from burial-mound sarcophagi and stone mortars.

detail.architecture: The keep of Himeji Castle is built with a timber frame, and the outer walls and the undersides of the eaves are coated with thick white plaster, which is both beautiful and fireproof; the joints of the roof tiles are also sealed with white plaster. The passages inside the castle are deliberately winding, and many gates are narrow and hidden, so invaders who wander around actually move away from the keep and are exposed to fire from the surrounding loopholes. The main keep is pierced from top to bottom by two central pillars about 25 meters long, which, together with the stone base about 15 meters high below, form a stable yet towering structure.
detail.visit: Himeji Castle is about a 20-minute walk from JR Himeji Station, and visitors can climb the main keep to see the interior timber frame; the adjacent Kōko-en Japanese garden is also worth a visit. It is most crowded during the cherry blossom season in early April, and weekday mornings are less crowded.

taj-mahal.name: Taj Mahal
taj-mahal.description: A white marble mausoleum built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his beloved wife Mumtaz Mahal, blending Persian, Islamic and Indian architectural styles.
facts: About 20,000 craftsmen were mobilized, and it took about 20 years to complete.
Gemstones from many places are inlaid in the marble.
The four minarets lean slightly outward so that they would fall away from the main tomb in an earthquake.

detail.overview: The Taj Mahal stands on the south bank of the Yamuna River at Agra in Uttar Pradesh, India. It is a mausoleum built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his beloved wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in childbirth in 1631. Work began in 1632, the main tomb was completed around 1643, and the whole complex was finished around 1653; the chief architect is generally held to be Ustad Ahmad Lahori. The tomb is built of pure white Makrana marble, its surface inlaid with stones of many colors, and combines Persian, Islamic and Indian architectural traditions in a display of perfect symmetry. It has been called "the jewel of Muslim art in India" and is the world's most famous monument to love.

stats.label: Main materials
stats.value: White marble (from Makrana, Rajasthan), red sandstone, gemstones

stats.label: Architectural style
stats.value: Mughal architecture (blending Persian, Islamic and Indian elements)

history.text: Empress Mumtaz Mahal dies giving birth to her 14th child at Burhanpur.
Shah Jahan orders a mausoleum built on the bank of the Yamuna at Agra, mobilizing about 20,000 craftsmen.
The main tomb is largely completed, and the mosque, forecourt and gateway continue to be built afterward.
The whole complex is largely finished.
Shah Jahan is deposed by his son Aurangzeb and in his old age is confined in Agra Fort, said to have been able only to gaze at the Taj Mahal from afar.
Shah Jahan dies and is buried beside Mumtaz Mahal in the mausoleum, the only arrangement in the building that breaks its symmetry.
A large-scale restoration directed by the British Indian viceroy Lord Curzon is completed, and he donates a large lamp for the interior.
Inscribed as a World Heritage Site.
Chosen as one of the "New Seven Wonders of the World."

parts.name: Main tomb
parts.description: A white marble mausoleum standing on a square platform, with tall iwan arches on each face; in the octagonal burial chamber inside are the cenotaphs of the two.

parts.name: Onion dome
parts.description: A large dome about 35 meters high crowns the main tomb, topped by a gilded finial and surrounded by four small kiosks.

parts.name: Minarets
parts.description: At each of the four corners of the platform stands a minaret about 40 meters high, leaning slightly outward so that if one fell it would not strike the main tomb.

parts.name: Mosque and jawab
parts.description: West of the main tomb is a red sandstone mosque, and to the east an identical-looking "jawab" (answer) building, which preserves the symmetry of the complex.

parts.name: Charbagh garden
parts.description: A Persian-style garden divided into four equal parts by waterways, symbolizing the four rivers of the Islamic paradise.

parts.name: Great gate
parts.description: The main red sandstone gate is inscribed with verses of the Quran, the letters growing larger toward the top so that they look the same size when seen from below.

parts.name: Crypt
parts.description: The real burial vault beneath the main tomb's chamber, where the bodies of Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal are buried.

detail.architecture: The Taj Mahal has a brick structural core faced with white marble, and by the pietra dura technique agate, jasper, lapis lazuli and other stones are inlaid in the marble to form floral and vine patterns. The whole complex is strictly symmetrical along the north–south axis, and the main tomb stands not in the middle of the garden but at the north end on the riverbank, so that visitors entering the gate see its complete outline set off against the sky. The marble changes color with the light: pink at dawn, pure white at noon, and silvery blue under moonlight.
detail.visit: The Taj Mahal is closed every Friday (open only to Muslims for prayer) and open from sunrise to sunset on the other days; entering the main tomb requires a separate ticket and shoe covers. To reduce pollution, the surroundings are regulated, and vehicles must park outside and visitors continue by electric vehicle.

eiffel.name: Eiffel Tower
eiffel.description: Built for the 1889 Paris World's Fair and the centennial of the French Revolution, it was at first harshly criticized by artists and has since become France's most representative landmark.
facts: It is made up of about 18,000 iron pieces and 2.5 million rivets.
In summer, heat expansion can raise the top by more than ten centimeters.
It was originally meant to stand for only 20 years, and was saved from demolition because it could serve as a radio antenna.

detail.overview: The Eiffel Tower stands on the Champ de Mars on the left bank of the Seine in Paris. It was built as the entrance landmark for the 1889 Paris World's Fair and the centennial of the French Revolution. The tower is named after the engineer Gustave Eiffel; it was conceived by engineers of his company, Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier, with the architect Stephen Sauvestre refining its appearance. It was completed in a little over two years and, at about 300 meters when finished, was the tallest man-made structure in the world, holding that record until 1930. During its construction many artists signed a protest, and it was originally permitted to remain for only 20 years; it was later preserved because of its value for radio communication, and it has now become the most representative symbol of France.

stats.label: Height
stats.value: About 330 m (including antenna; about 300 m when completed)

stats.label: Base
stats.value: Four legs enclose a square about 125 m on each side

stats.label: Weight
stats.value: About 7,300 tonnes of ironwork, about 10,100 tonnes in total

stats.label: Purpose
stats.value: World's Fair landmark, observation decks, radio and television transmission tower

history.text: Koechlin and Nouguier come up with the initial idea for the tower, and Eiffel then buys the design patent.
Work begins on the tower's foundations; in February of the same year a number of artists publish the protest letter "Against the Eiffel Tower" in the press.
The tower is completed, and Eiffel climbs to the top to raise the French flag.
The tower opens to visitors with the World's Fair, drawing nearly 2 million people to climb it during the fair.
The originally planned 20-year permit expires, and it is allowed to remain because of its value as a radio transmitter.
The Chrysler Building in New York is completed, and the tower loses its status as the world's tallest man-made structure.
A television antenna is added, raising the height to about 320 meters.
Inscribed as a World Heritage Site as part of "Paris, Banks of the Seine."
A digital broadcasting antenna is added, raising the height to about 330 meters.

parts.name: Four legs
parts.description: Four curved piers of latticed steel, each oriented to a cardinal direction, fixed at the base on concrete and masonry foundations.

parts.name: First level
parts.description: About 57 meters above the ground, with partly transparent glass floor sections and restaurants, overlooking the plaza beneath the tower.

parts.name: Second level
parts.description: About 116 meters above the ground, one of the observation levels with the best views, with a Michelin-class restaurant.

parts.name: Top level
parts.description: An observation deck about 276 meters above the ground, preserving a reconstruction of Eiffel's original office.

parts.name: Elevator system
parts.description: Elevators within the legs run diagonally along the curve, and from the second level one changes to an elevator going directly to the top.

parts.name: Stairs
parts.description: About 1,665 steps from the ground to the top; ordinary visitors can walk up to the second level (about 674 steps).

parts.name: Antennas and transmission equipment
parts.description: Broadcasting and television antennas are mounted at the top, continuing the tower's communications role since the early 20th century.

detail.architecture: The Eiffel Tower uses an openwork lattice structure, assembling triangular trusses from a great many small iron pieces to achieve high strength at very light weight and greatly reduce wind pressure. The curve of the tower was calculated for wind resistance so that the bending moment caused by wind is carried down the legs to the ground. All the components were precisely prefabricated in the factory with rivet holes already made and then shipped to the site for assembly, so construction took only two years and two months. The tower is repainted about every seven years, each time requiring about 60 tonnes of paint to prevent rust.
detail.visit: The Eiffel Tower is open all year, and visitors can ascend by elevator or climb the stairs; it is recommended to buy timed tickets in advance on the official website to reduce waiting in line. After dark it sparkles with lights for about five minutes on the hour, one of the highlights of Paris at night.

pisa.name: Leaning Tower of Pisa
pisa.description: The freestanding bell tower of Pisa Cathedral, which began to lean soon after construction began because of the soft soil under its foundations and took nearly two hundred years to complete; the world's most famous "architectural blunder."
facts: It began to lean about five years after construction started, when it had reached the third level, and the long suspension of work caused by wars actually gave the foundations time to compact so that it did not collapse.
It was closed in 1990 with a tilt of about 5.5 degrees and, after 11 years of soil extraction, was straightened by about 45 centimeters, reopening in 2001.
The story of Galileo performing falling-body experiments from the tower is widely told, but historians think it is very likely only a legend.

detail.overview: The Leaning Tower of Pisa is the freestanding bell tower of the cathedral of Pisa, Italy, and together with the cathedral, the baptistery and the cemetery forms the "Piazza dei Miracoli" complex. Medieval Pisa was a wealthy and powerful maritime republic, and its citizens used the riches brought back from naval victories to build this magnificent group of white marble buildings, displaying the strength of the city-state. Work on the bell tower began in 1173, but beneath its foundations lay soft clay and sand, and it began to lean when it reached the third level; it was then suspended several times because of wars, taking nearly two hundred years in all to complete. Its tilt threatened its safety in the late 20th century, and only after more than ten years of rescue work by international experts did it reach its stable condition today.

stats.label: Height
stats.value: About 55.86 m on the low side, about 56.67 m on the high side

stats.label: Angle of tilt
stats.value: About 4 degrees (about 5.5 degrees before the 1990 closure)

stats.label: Stories and steps
stats.value: 8 levels in all, with a spiral staircase of about 294–296 steps

history.text: The Pisan fleet defeats Muslim forces at Palermo, and the spoils fund the start of work on the cathedral, beginning the construction of the Piazza dei Miracoli.
Work on the bell tower begins in August, with foundations only about 3 meters deep, built on soft alluvial soil.
When the third level is reached the tower begins to lean to the north; Pisa then goes to war with Genoa and other city-states, and construction stops for nearly a hundred years.
Giovanni di Simone resumes construction, deliberately making the upper floors lean toward the opposite side to offset the tilt, which gives the tower a slight curve.
The topmost bell chamber is completed and seven large bells are installed, and the whole bell tower is finally finished.
According to Galileo's student Viviani, Galileo dropped balls of different weights from the tower to show that falling bodies land together, but most historians think this is a legend.
An architect digs a walkway around the base to reveal the buried foundations, allowing groundwater to seep in and aggravating the tilt.
With the tilt at about 5.5 degrees and the top displaced by more than 4 meters, the Italian government orders it closed and sets up an international committee of experts to rescue it.

By extracting soil from beneath the north side of the foundations, the tower is straightened by about 45 centimeters and reopens to climbing; in 2008 it is confirmed that the tower has stopped moving.

parts.name: Foundations
parts.description: A ring-shaped stone foundation about 15.5 meters in diameter and only about 3 meters deep, sitting on a soft clay layer, the root cause of the tilt.

parts.name: Ground-level blind arcade
parts.description: The outer wall of the first level is decorated with 15 engaged columns and blind arches, without an open gallery.

parts.name: Open colonnades
parts.description: Levels two through seven each have a surrounding ring of arcaded columns, stacked one above another, forming the leaning tower's most characteristic appearance.

parts.name: Bell chamber
parts.description: The top level completed in 1372, smaller in diameter, containing seven large bells, each corresponding to one note of the musical scale.

parts.name: Spiral staircase
parts.description: The staircase winds upward hidden inside the thick wall, and when climbing one clearly feels the disorientation brought on by the tilt.

parts.name: Hollow core
parts.description: The interior of the tower is a cylindrical space running from top to bottom, so that one can look straight up to the top from the base.

parts.name: Piazza dei Miracoli
parts.description: The white marble complex made up of the leaning tower together with the cathedral, the baptistery and the Camposanto cemetery.

detail.architecture: The leaning tower is a typical Pisan Romanesque building of white marble with gray stripes, its exterior made up of stacked round-arched colonnades in harmony with the style of the neighboring cathedral. Because it had begun to lean while still under construction, later builders deliberately built the upper levels higher on one side, so the tower is not straight but slightly curved. The rescue work of the 1990s first added lead weights to the north-side foundation and held the tower with steel cables, then used angled drilling to extract soil bit by bit from beneath the north foundation, letting the tower slowly straighten under its own weight.
detail.visit: The leaning tower is open for climbing; to protect the structure, timed reservations are required and the number of people per group is limited, and children under 8 may not climb. The cathedral on the piazza can be visited free of charge, while the baptistery and cemetery require tickets.

belem-tower.name: Belém Tower
belem-tower.description: A defensive tower built by King Manuel I to guard the mouth of the Tagus River and also the gateway for fleets entering and leaving Lisbon in the Age of Discovery, symbolizing Portugal's maritime supremacy.
facts: A rhinoceros is carved on the outer wall, inspired by the rhinoceros that arrived in Lisbon from India in 1515, considered one of the earliest rhinoceros sculptures in Europe.
When it was built the tower stood on a rock in the river, but with silting of the riverbank and land reclamation it now lies almost against the north bank.
Inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1983 together with the nearby Jerónimos Monastery.

detail.overview: Belém Tower stands in the Belém district of western Lisbon and is formally named the "Tower of Saint Vincent," after Lisbon's patron saint. In the late 15th century King John II of Portugal planned a system of defenses at the mouth of the Tagus, and his successor Manuel I, backed by the wealth brought by the Age of Discovery, built this tower to guard the river mouth and to serve as a ceremonial gateway for fleets entering and leaving. The tower is decorated with many knotted ropes, armillary spheres and crosses of the Order of Christ, symbols of seafaring and royal power, and is a leading work of "Manueline" architecture. It bore witness to Portugal's rise and fall from maritime power to annexation by Spain, and is now one of the most important symbols of Portugal's Age of Discovery.

stats.label: Structure
stats.value: A four-story square tower with a polygonal bulwark battery in front

stats.label: Architectural style
stats.value: Manueline (late Gothic blended with Renaissance and Moorish elements)

history.text: King John II plans to guard the mouth of the Tagus with several fortresses, protecting the capital Lisbon from attack from the sea.
Vasco da Gama leads a fleet from the Belém area and reaches India the following year, opening Portugal's sea route to Asia.
Manuel I orders the tower built, with the architect Francisco de Arruda, who had worked on fortress projects in North Africa, in charge.
The rhinoceros sent from India arrives in Lisbon, causing a sensation in Europe, and the rhinoceros sculpture on the west side of the tower was inspired by it.
Belém Tower is largely completed, becoming a ceremonial gateway and defensive fortress for the fleets of the Age of Discovery entering and leaving Lisbon.

In the Portuguese succession crisis, Spanish troops enter Lisbon and the garrison of Belém Tower surrenders; during the sixty years of shared monarchy that followed, the dungeon in the tower is used as a prison.
Belém Tower is restored with some new Neo-Manueline decoration added, and thereafter gradually changes from a military installation into a historic monument.
Inscribed as a World Heritage Site together with the Jerónimos Monastery.
Chosen by public vote as one of the "Seven Wonders of Portugal."

parts.name: Bulwark battery
parts.description: A polygonal platform projecting into the river in front of the tower, with gun ports in the walls, the main source of firepower defending the river mouth.

parts.name: Square tower
parts.description: A four-story tower about 30 meters high, containing in order the governor's chamber, the King's Chamber, the audience room and the chapel, with a terrace on top overlooking the river mouth.

parts.name: King's Chamber balcony
parts.description: A Renaissance-style loggia balcony facing the river, from which the king could watch the fleets set sail.

parts.name: Rhinoceros sculpture
parts.description: A stone gargoyle at the corner of the west wall, considered one of the earliest rhinoceros sculptures in Europe.

parts.name: Battlements and cross shields
parts.description: The battlements are decorated with shields bearing the cross of the Order of Christ, which funded and took part in Portugal's voyages of exploration.

parts.name: Statue of the Virgin
parts.description: A statue of the Virgin and Child on the bulwark facing the river mouth, symbolizing prayers for the safe return of sailors.

parts.name: Dungeon
parts.description: The space on the bulwark's lowest level was originally a magazine and was later turned into a prison, into which seawater seeps at high tide.

detail.architecture: Belém Tower combines the square tower of a medieval castle with the then-new gun battery bastion, reflecting the change in fortifications in the age of artillery. Its walls are carved in white limestone with Manueline decoration such as ropes, armillary spheres, crosses and marine creatures, turning a military building into a work of art proclaiming royal power and maritime achievement. The small lookout turrets of the tower, with domes and pointed arches, show the influence of Moorish architecture of North Africa.
detail.visit: Belém Tower is open to visitors, and one can climb to the rooftop terrace to look out over the Tagus, but the stairs inside the tower are narrow and numbers are controlled. The nearby Jerónimos Monastery and the Monument to the Discoveries are within walking distance and make a good combined visit.

statue-of-liberty.name: Statue of Liberty
statue-of-liberty.location: United States · Liberty Island, New York
statue-of-liberty.description: A colossal copper statue presented by the people of France to celebrate the centennial of American independence and the friendship between the two nations, formally titled "Liberty Enlightening the World," and the first landmark seen by countless immigrants arriving in America.
facts: The sculptor Bartholdi designed its exterior, while the internal iron framework was the work of Gustave Eiffel, who built the Eiffel Tower.
The copper skin is only about 2.4 millimeters thick; it was originally copper-colored and turned the blue-green seen today only after oxidation.
The tablet in the left hand is inscribed with the date of American independence, "JULY IV MDCCLXXVI" (July 4, 1776).

detail.overview: The Statue of Liberty stands on Liberty Island in New York Harbor; its formal title is "Liberty Enlightening the World," and it is a gift from the people of France to the United States. The idea was proposed by the French scholar Édouard de Laboulaye after the end of the American Civil War, with the aim of celebrating the centennial of American independence, the Union victory and the abolition of slavery, and also of expressing hopes for France's own pursuit of republican liberty. The statue was designed by the sculptor Bartholdi, with Eiffel responsible for the internal iron framework, while the American side was responsible for funding the construction of the pedestal. After its unveiling in 1886 it became a symbol welcoming millions of immigrants, representing liberty, democracy and the hope of a new life.

stats.label: Height of the statue
stats.value: About 46 m (from the base of the feet to the tip of the torch)

stats.label: Total height
stats.value: About 93 m (including the pedestal and foundation)

stats.label: Weight
stats.value: About 27 tonnes of copper and about 113 tonnes of steel

stats.label: Steps to the crown
stats.value: About 354 steps from the pedestal to the crown

history.text: The French scholar Laboulaye proposes that the people of France present a monument to the United States to celebrate the centennial of American independence and the friendship between the two countries.
The completed right arm and torch are exhibited at the Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia, where visitors can pay to climb the torch, raising funds for the construction.
The statue is assembled in Paris and formally handed over to the American side; in the same year work on the pedestal begins on Bedloe's Island (now Liberty Island) in New York.

Work on the pedestal stalls for lack of funds, and the publisher Joseph Pulitzer launches a fundraising drive in the New York World that draws donations from more than 120,000 people; the statue is dismantled into 350 pieces, crated and shipped to New York.
On October 28 the unveiling ceremony is presided over by U.S. President Grover Cleveland.
The poem "The New Colossus" by the poet Emma Lazarus is cast on a bronze plaque and placed inside the pedestal; "Give me your tired, your poor" becomes a famous line expressing the immigrant spirit.
German saboteurs blow up a munitions depot on nearby Black Tom Island, causing a huge explosion that damages the statue's arm; thereafter the public is no longer allowed to climb up into the torch.
Designated a National Monument by the U.S. government.
A large-scale restoration is carried out in preparation for the centennial, replacing the rusted internal iron bars and substituting a new gold-leaf-covered torch for the original.

parts.name: Torch
parts.description: The raised right hand holds a torch, symbolizing the light of liberty illuminating the world; the present flame is covered in gold leaf, and the original torch is displayed in the museum on the island.

parts.name: Crown
parts.description: The crown has 7 rays, often interpreted as symbolizing the seven continents or seven seas, with 25 windows inside from which to look out over New York Harbor.

parts.name: Tablet
parts.description: The tablet held in the left arm is inscribed with the Roman numerals "JULY IV MDCCLXXVI," the date of the American Declaration of Independence, July 4, 1776.

parts.name: Broken chains
parts.description: At the goddess's feet lie broken chains and shackles, symbolizing release from oppression and bondage, not easy to see from the ground.

parts.name: Iron framework
parts.description: Eiffel's central iron pylon and secondary framework, which let the copper skin move slightly with temperature and wind without cracking.

parts.name: Granite pedestal
parts.description: Designed by the architect Hunt and built of concrete and granite, it was one of the largest concrete structures in the United States at the time.

parts.name: Fort Wood
parts.description: The eleven-pointed star-shaped fort beneath the statue's pedestal, originally a military fortress guarding New York Harbor in the early 19th century.

detail.architecture: The Statue of Liberty uses the repoussé technique: craftsmen first made wooden molds, then hammered thin copper sheets into shape piece by piece and finally riveted them to the iron-bar grid inside. Eiffel's structure keeps the outer copper skin from bearing load directly, instead hanging it on the framework like skin, free to expand and contract with heat and strong wind. Over several decades the copper skin reacted with the air to form blue-green verdigris, and this patina in fact protects the copper beneath.
detail.visit: To reach Liberty Island one must take a ferry from Battery Park in Manhattan or Liberty State Park in New Jersey, and climbing the pedestal and crown requires advance reservations. The Statue of Liberty Museum on the island opened in 2019 and displays the original torch.

moai.name: Moai Statues
moai.description: Giant figures carved by the Rapa Nui people from volcanic tuff, representing deified ancestors; Ahu Tongariki is the largest platform on the island, with 15 restored moai raised again.
facts: There are more than nine hundred moai on the island in all, the great majority from the quarry on the Rano Raraku volcano.
The statues at Tongariki had all fallen, and in 1960 they were scattered by the tsunami set off by the great Chilean earthquake; they were restored only in the 1990s.
Most moai have their backs to the sea and face the village, symbolizing the ancestors watching over the people.

detail.overview: The moai are giant stone statues on Easter Island (called Rapa Nui locally) in the South Pacific, carved by the island's Polynesian inhabitants. Scholars believe the moai represent deified ancestors, standing on stone ceremonial platforms called "ahu," most with their backs to the sea and facing the village, symbolizing the ancestors' spiritual power protecting the people. Ahu Tongariki is the island's largest ahu; its 15 moai all fell over at some point in history and were then scattered by a tsunami, and they were restored only in the 1990s through cooperation between Chile and Japan. These statues bear witness to the astonishing craftsmanship developed by an isolated island society in an environment of limited resources.

stats.label: Heaviest statue
stats.value: About 86 tonnes (the heaviest moai ever raised on the island)

stats.label: Number of moai on the island
Main materials
stats.value: Tuff from the Rano Raraku volcano; topknots of red volcanic scoria

history.text: Polynesian navigators reach one of the most isolated inhabited islands in the Pacific by canoe; the exact date is still debated among scholars.
The clans quarry and carve moai at the Rano Raraku volcano, transport them to the ahu on the coast and erect them; Tongariki is also expanded in stages in this period.
The Dutch explorer Jacob Roggeveen arrives on Easter Day, the first European to visit, which gives the island its name.

When the British explorer Cook visits he already sees some moai that have fallen; by the mid-19th century almost all the statues on the island have been toppled, possibly because of clan conflict and social upheaval.
Peruvian slave traders carry off about 1,500 islanders, and together with introduced diseases the population falls sharply, causing much oral knowledge to be lost.
Chile annexes Easter Island.
The Valdivia earthquake in Chile triggers a tsunami that sweeps the fallen statues of Tongariki several tens of meters inland.
Restoration is directed by the Chilean archaeologist Claudio Cristino, with the Japanese crane company Tadano providing cranes and funding, and the 15 moai are raised again.
A wildfire breaks out around Rano Raraku, burning and damaging some moai and drawing attention to the protection of cultural heritage.

parts.name: Moai Statues
parts.description: Half-length figures with disproportionately large heads, long ears, deep eye sockets and tightly closed lips; the 15 statues at Tongariki differ in height and build.

parts.name: Ahu platform
parts.description: A long, narrow ceremonial platform built of dressed stone, often with ancestral remains buried beneath it, serving as the base on which the moai stand.

parts.name: Pukao topknot
parts.description: A cylindrical topknot carved from the red volcanic scoria of the Puna Pau quarry; one of the moai at Tongariki wears a pukao.

parts.name: Eyes
parts.description: After a moai was erected, eyes made of coral and obsidian or red scoria were inserted, thought to "activate" the ancestor's spiritual power.

parts.name: Rano Raraku quarry
parts.description: A volcanic crater not far from Tongariki, source of about ninety percent of the island's moai, where hundreds of unfinished or untransported statues still remain on the slopes.

parts.name: Paved plaza
parts.description: A plaza paved with stones in front of the ahu, a space for ceremonies and gatherings.

detail.architecture: Craftsmen carved the statues directly into the softer tuff cliff face with hard basalt stone tools, and only after completion detached them from the rock face and transported them down the mountain. There are still various accounts of how the statues were transported; one experiment showed that pulling with ropes from both sides can make an upright moai rock from side to side and "walk" to its destination, matching the islanders' legend that "the moai walked there themselves." The ahu platforms were built of precisely cut stones fitted together, and the fineness of workmanship in some of the walls is astonishing.
detail.visit: The moai sites on Easter Island belong to Rapa Nui National Park, which is managed with the participation of the indigenous community; visitors must buy a park ticket, and some sites must be visited with a qualified guide. Tongariki is a popular place to watch the sunrise, and touching or climbing the statues is prohibited.

callanish.name: Callanish Standing Stones
callanish.location: United Kingdom · Isle of Lewis, Outer Hebrides, Scotland
callanish.description: A Neolithic stone complex on a remote island in northwest Scotland, with a central stone circle at its core and cruciform rows of stones extending outward; it is older than the large sarsen circle of Stonehenge.
facts: The stone is Lewisian gneiss, one of the oldest rocks on Earth, about 3 billion years old.
It was buried under about 1.5 meters of peat, and its full form was revealed only after the peat was cleared in 1857.
During the "major lunar standstill," which occurs once every 18.6 years, the moon skims low over the southern ridge behind the stones.

detail.overview: The Callanish Standing Stones stand on the west coast of the Isle of Lewis in the Outer Hebrides of Scotland and are among the best-preserved and most spectacular prehistoric stone monuments in Britain. They were raised by a Neolithic farming community about five thousand years ago: a central stone circle forms the core, with an avenue of stones extending north and a row of stones reaching out to the east, south and west, so that from the air the whole looks like a cross. Scholars believe this may have been a place for ritual and for observing the heavens, especially during the "major lunar standstill" that occurs once every 18.6 years, when the moon skims low over the southern ridge. The stones were later buried under peat for thousands of years and came to light again only in the 19th century.

stats.label: Builders
stats.value: Neolithic farming inhabitants of the Isle of Lewis

stats.label: Central stone circle
stats.value: 13 standing stones, about 13 m in diameter

stats.label: Main materials
stats.value: Lewisian gneiss (ancient rock about 3 billion years old)

stats.label: Layout
stats.value: Stone circle plus four rows of stones, forming a cross

history.text: Neolithic farmers have settled and farmed on the Isle of Lewis, and the area becomes an important settlement and ritual center.
The inhabitants raise the central monolith and the stone circle and gradually add the outward-extending avenue and stone rows.
A small chambered tomb is built inside the stone circle beside the central monolith, used for burial.
In the early Bronze Age the chambered tomb is still reused, and is later damaged and remodeled, showing that the use of the site changed with the times.
The climate turns cold and wet, the site is gradually abandoned, and peat begins to build up and slowly bury the lower part of the standing stones.
The Scottish writer Martin Martin describes the standing stones in A Description of the Western Islands of Scotland; local legend says they are giants who refused conversion and were turned to stone.
The landowner of Lewis, Sir James Matheson, orders the peat cleared, about 1.5 meters thick, and the full form of the stones and the central chambered tomb are revealed again.
Archaeologists carry out systematic excavation at the site, clarifying the sequence in which the stone circle and the chambered tomb were built.
During the major lunar standstill cycle, researchers and visitors from many places come to observe the alignment of the moon with the stones.

parts.name: Central monolith
parts.description: A slender standing stone about 4.8 meters high at the center of the circle, the visual focus of the whole site.

parts.name: Central stone circle
parts.description: A slightly flattened ring of 13 standing stones, about 13 meters in diameter.

parts.name: North avenue
parts.description: A passage about 83 meters long made of two parallel rows of standing stones, extending north-northeast from the stone circle.

parts.name: East, south and west rows
parts.description: Three single rows of standing stones extend outward from the circle and, with the north avenue, form a cross-shaped layout; the south row is aligned roughly due south.

parts.name: Chambered tomb
parts.description: A small burial chamber built inside the circle on the east side of the central monolith, later in date than the circle and discovered only after the peat was cleared in the 19th century.

parts.name: Surrounding stone circles
parts.description: Within a few kilometers are more than ten smaller stone circles and standing stones, showing that this area was an important ritual landscape in prehistory.

detail.architecture: The standing stones at Callanish are of local Lewisian gneiss, and the stones were not heavily dressed, keeping their natural slab-like shapes and wavy rock texture. Most of the standing stones have their narrow faces toward the center of the circle, and their alignments were deliberately planned, with the south row pointing roughly due south, which scholars believe relates to the movements of the sun and moon. When raised, the stones' bases were buried in the ground and packed with rubble, which is why they have stood for thousands of years without falling.
detail.visit: The Callanish Standing Stones are open free of charge all year, and visitors can walk freely among the stones and observe them up close. The nearby visitor center explains the history of the site and related legends; to get there one must first take a ferry or plane to the Isle of Lewis.

hagia-sophia.name: Hagia Sophia
hagia-sophia.description: A great church built by the Byzantine emperor Justinian I, which astonished the world with its unprecedentedly huge dome; converted into a mosque after 1453 and later a museum, it has witnessed the succession of Christian and Islamic civilizations.
facts: It was completed in only about five years and ten months, and for nearly a thousand years was the largest cathedral in the world.
Forty windows ring the base of the dome, so that the light makes the dome appear to float in the air.
It was converted into a museum in 1934 and restored to use as a mosque in 2020.

detail.overview: Hagia Sophia stands in the old city of Istanbul (anciently Constantinople), and its name means "Holy Wisdom." The present building was reconstructed on the order of the Byzantine emperor Justinian I after the Nika riots burned the earlier church, in order to display the glory of imperial power and of the Christian empire. Its huge central dome created an interior space of unprecedented breadth, and for nearly a thousand years it was the largest cathedral in the world and the center of the Orthodox faith. After the Ottoman Empire captured Constantinople in 1453 it became a mosque, in 1934 a museum, and in 2020 a mosque again, and its changes of status reflect the history of this city between Eastern and Western civilizations.

stats.label: Architects
stats.value: Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus

stats.label: Dimensions of the main body
stats.value: About 82 m long and 73 m wide

stats.label: Main materials
stats.value: Brick, mortar, colored marble brought from many places

history.text: The first Hagia Sophia is dedicated by Emperor Constantius II, a rectangular basilica with a timber roof, later destroyed in the riots of 404.
The Nika riots burn the second church; after suppressing the riots Justinian I immediately orders it rebuilt on an unprecedented scale.
On December 27 the new church is dedicated; Justinian is said to have exclaimed on entering, "Solomon, I have surpassed you!"
After an earthquake the original dome collapses and is rebuilt by Isidore the Younger with a higher curvature, rededicated in 562, which is the basis of the dome seen today.
Papal legates place a bull of excommunication against the Patriarch of Constantinople on the church's altar, and the Great Schism between the Eastern and Western churches begins.
The Fourth Crusade captures Constantinople and sacks the church extensively; for nearly sixty years afterward it becomes a Latin Catholic church.
The Ottoman sultan Mehmed II captures Constantinople and converts the church into a mosque, and four minarets are added over the following years.
The Republic of Turkey under Atatürk's government converts it into a museum, opened the following year, and the covered Byzantine mosaics gradually come to light again.
A Turkish court annuls its museum status, and the government announces its restoration as a mosque; on July 24 the first Friday prayers in 86 years are held.

parts.name: Central great dome
parts.description: A shallow-curved dome about 55.6 meters high with 40 windows ringing its base, so that the light makes the dome seem to float in the air.

parts.name: Pendentives
parts.description: Four curved triangular surfaces that transfer the weight above the square space to four huge piers, allowing a circular dome to be set on a square plan.

parts.name: Semi-domes
parts.description: On the east and west sides of the great dome are semi-domes, followed outward by smaller semi-domes, forming a broad nave that extends in successive tiers.

parts.name: Upper gallery
parts.description: Originally the galleries from which women and empresses watched ceremonies, preserving masterpieces of Byzantine art such as the 13th-century Deësis mosaic.

parts.name: Mihrab and minbar
parts.description: Added after conversion to a mosque; the mihrab points toward Mecca, and the minbar is the raised platform from which the imam delivers sermons.

parts.name: Minarets
parts.description: Four minarets added in the Ottoman period, built during the reigns of different sultans and not identical in form.

parts.name: Calligraphic roundels
parts.description: Eight giant roundels hung in the nave in the 19th century, inscribed in Arabic calligraphy with the names of Allah, the Prophet Muhammad and the early caliphs.
