detail.architecture: Hagia Sophia combines a rectangular basilica with a centralized dome and solves the problem of setting a huge dome on a square plan with pendentives, becoming a model of Byzantine architecture. The dome is built of lightweight brick and thick mortar, and the outward thrust is shared by the semi-domes and huge buttresses; the Ottoman architect Sinan strengthened the exterior buttresses in the 16th century, allowing the building to survive many earthquakes. It also deeply influenced later Ottoman mosques, such as the Blue Mosque opposite.
detail.visit: Hagia Sophia is currently in use as a mosque, and sightseeing entry is suspended during prayer times; visitors must remove their shoes on entering, and women must cover their heads. Since 2024 foreign visitors must buy tickets and go by a separate entrance to visit the upper gallery.

florence-duomo.name: Florence Cathedral (Santa Maria del Fiore)
florence-duomo.description: The cathedral of Florence, whose great red-brick dome was built by Brunelleschi with innovative methods, regarded as the beginning of Renaissance architecture and the most striking landmark of the city.
facts: The dome has an internal diameter of about 45.5 meters and is still the largest brick dome in the world.
Brunelleschi completed the dome without traditional wooden centering, using a double shell and herringbone brickwork.
The facade was not completed until 1887, in the Neo-Gothic style.

detail.overview: Santa Maria del Fiore is the cathedral of Florence and, with Giotto's Campanile and the Baptistery of San Giovanni, forms the cathedral piazza complex. Florence at the end of the 13th century grew rich through the wool trade and banking, and the city government decided to build a cathedral that would surpass those of rival cities such as Pisa and Siena. The cathedral's design left room for a huge octagonal dome, but its span was so great that no one at the time knew how to build it, and it stood open for decades until Brunelleschi completed it by revolutionary methods. The dome is not only an engineering marvel but is also seen as the starting point of the Renaissance.

stats.label: Architects
stats.value: Arnolfo di Cambio (began the work), Brunelleschi (dome)

history.text: The architect Arnolfo di Cambio directs the start of work, building a new cathedral on the site of the old church of Santa Reparata.
The painter Giotto is appointed master of the works and designs the campanile, which is later completed by Andrea Pisano and Talenti.
The Wool Guild holds a competition for the dome's design, and Brunelleschi defeats Ghiberti and other rivals with a proposal that does not use wooden centering.
Work on the dome proceeds, with Brunelleschi inventing a variety of hoisting machines at the same time; on March 25, 1436, Pope Eugene IV consecrates the cathedral.

After Brunelleschi's death the lantern is completed according to his design; in 1471 a gilded copper ball cast by Verrocchio is placed on top of the lantern, while the young Leonardo da Vinci was training in his workshop.
The Pazzi family plots to assassinate the Medici brothers during Mass; Giuliano is killed, while Lorenzo is wounded but escapes.
Vasari and Zuccari paint the huge fresco of the Last Judgment on the inside of the dome.
The unfinished medieval facade is demolished, and for a long time afterward the front of the cathedral has only a rough wall.
The Neo-Gothic polychrome marble facade designed by the architect Emilio De Fabris is unveiled, and the cathedral's exterior is finally completed.

parts.name: Brunelleschi's dome
parts.description: An octagonal double dome of red brick, with eight white stone ribs converging from the base to the top, the focal point of the Florence skyline.

parts.name: Lantern and golden ball
parts.description: The white marble lantern at the top of the dome both weighs down the dome structure and lets light into the interior, topped by a gilded copper ball and a cross.

parts.name: Giotto's Campanile
parts.description: A freestanding bell tower about 84.7 meters high, its outer walls patterned in white, green and pink marble to echo the cathedral's exterior.

parts.name: Baptistery of San Giovanni
parts.description: The octagonal building opposite the cathedral, whose east doors, made by Ghiberti, are the bronze doors that Michelangelo praised as the "Gates of Paradise."

parts.name: Neo-Gothic facade
parts.description: A splendid front completed in the 19th century, in white, green and pink marble with statues and mosaics.

parts.name: Fresco of the Last Judgment
parts.description: A masterpiece of about 3,600 square meters painted on the inside of the dome, one of the largest frescoes in the world.

parts.name: Santa Reparata excavations
parts.description: Beneath the cathedral are preserved the remains of its predecessor, the church of Santa Reparata, and Brunelleschi's tomb is also located here.

detail.architecture: Brunelleschi made the dome of two shells, inner and outer, with passages and stairways left between them, both lightening the weight and strengthening the structure. With his herringbone brickwork each ring of bricks locks against the next, so the dome could support itself during construction without the need for huge wooden centering; at the base of the dome he also embedded a hoop of stone and iron chains to resist the outward thrust. The body of the church belongs to Italian Gothic, which, compared with northern Gothic churches, emphasizes broad, horizontal space and polychrome marble outer walls.
detail.visit: The church itself can be entered free of charge, but climbing the dome and the campanile, and visiting the Baptistery and the Opera del Duomo Museum, require a combined ticket and a reserved time slot for the dome climb. On the way up the dome one can see the Last Judgment fresco close up, and from the top one can look out over all of Florence.

neuschwanstein.name: Neuschwanstein Castle
neuschwanstein.description: A fairy-tale castle created by King Ludwig II of Bavaria, inspired by medieval chivalric legends and Wagner's operas; unfinished when the king died, it is now one of Germany's most popular tourist castles.
facts: The king lived in the castle for only about 172 days, and it opened to visitors just seven weeks after his death.
Its exterior imitates the Middle Ages, but inside it had the new technology of the time, such as central heating, running water and telephones.
It is often said to be one of the inspirations for the Sleeping Beauty Castle at Disneyland.

detail.overview: Neuschwanstein Castle stands at Schwangau in the foothills of the Alps in southern Bavaria, on a cliff above the Pöllat Gorge. After Bavaria's defeat in the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 and the limiting of his royal powers, King Ludwig II of Bavaria became increasingly immersed in the world of medieval knights and Germanic legends and decided to build an ideal knightly castle, also as a tribute to the composer Wagner, whom he admired. The castle's exterior imitates the Middle Ages, but in fact it was built with the most advanced technology of the day, designed with the involvement of a stage designer and full of theatrical romanticism. The king died mysteriously before the castle was finished, and this unfinished dream castle has instead become one of Germany's best-known tourist landmarks.

stats.label: Designers
stats.value: Stage designer Christian Jank, architect Eduard Riedel and others

stats.label: Construction cost
stats.value: More than 6.2 million marks (far over budget)

history.text: The 18-year-old Ludwig II takes the throne as King of Bavaria and soon invites Wagner to Munich and funds his work.
Bavaria fights on Austria's side in the Austro-Prussian War and is defeated, forced into an alliance with Prussia, and the king's real power is greatly reduced.
The king visits the Wartburg in Germany and the Château de Pierrefonds in France, which become important inspirations for the design of Neuschwanstein.
On September 5 a foundation-stone ceremony is held on the site of the old castle ruins, and the hilltop is blasted flat to build the new castle.
The gatehouse is the first to be completed, and the king lived in the gatehouse to supervise the work while the main building was under construction.
The king moves into the still-unfinished main palace building, but in all he lived there for only about 172 days.
In June the king is declared insane and deposed, and the day after being taken from the castle he drowns in Lake Starnberg; on August 1 of the same year the castle opens to visitors.
During World War II the Nazis store large quantities of artworks looted from France and elsewhere in the castle, and they are recovered by the Allies after the war.
Inscribed as a World Heritage Site, together with Linderhof Palace, Herrenchiemsee and the Schachen royal house, as the "Palaces of Ludwig II of Bavaria."

parts.name: Gatehouse
parts.description: The red-brick building at the castle entrance, the first to be completed, where the king lived for many years.

parts.name: Palace main building
parts.description: The main building of the castle, containing the king's living quarters and the principal halls, with towers and spires set at varying heights to form a fairy-tale silhouette.

parts.name: Throne Hall
parts.description: A two-story hall modeled on a Byzantine church, with a golden dome and huge chandelier of extraordinary splendor, but the throne had not been completed when the king died and it still stands empty today.

parts.name: Singers' Hall
parts.description: Modeled on the singers' hall of the Wartburg, its walls are covered with paintings of the legend of the Grail knight Parsifal, one of the spaces the king valued most.

parts.name: King's bedroom
parts.description: A bedroom decorated with elaborate Neo-Gothic wood carving, with murals depicting the story of Wagner's opera Tristan and Isolde.

parts.name: Artificial grotto
parts.description: A stalactite cave setting between the bedroom and the living room, inspired by the Venusberg grotto in the opera Tannhäuser.

parts.name: Marienbrücke (Mary's Bridge)
parts.description: An iron bridge spanning the Pöllat Gorge, the classic vantage point for a view of the whole of Neuschwanstein.

detail.architecture: The exterior of Neuschwanstein imitates a medieval Romanesque castle, but its interior is mainly of brick faced with limestone and uses industrial-age materials such as steel beams. The castle was equipped with central heating, running water on every floor, flush toilets, electric bells and telephones, and the kitchen had an automatically rotating spit and dumbwaiter, making it a very modern residence for its time. It was not built for defense but is a "historicist" building that brought the stage of Wagner's operas into the real world.
detail.visit: The interior of the castle can only be visited by guided tour at reserved times, and tickets in peak season often sell out in advance, so it is advisable to book online beforehand. From the village of Hohenschwangau at the foot of the hill one can walk, take a shuttle bus or a horse-drawn carriage up the hill, and Marienbrücke is a popular spot for photographing the whole castle.

louvre.name: The Louvre
louvre.style: French Renaissance and classical palace, modern glass architecture
louvre.description: From medieval fortress and French royal palace to the world's largest art museum, the Louvre has been expanded over more than eight hundred years; the glass pyramid by I. M. Pei, completed in 1989, lets the ancient palace converse with modern architecture.
facts: Opened as a public museum in 1793 during the French Revolution, it is the most visited museum in the world.
Its collection includes masterpieces such as the Mona Lisa, the Venus de Milo and the Winged Victory of Samothrace.
The glass pyramid is made of 673 panes of glass and provoked fierce controversy when it was first completed.

detail.overview: The Louvre stands on the right bank of the Seine in central Paris and was originally a fortress built in the late 12th century by King Philip II of France to defend Paris. Successive kings thereafter kept rebuilding and enlarging it into a splendid royal palace, until after Louis XIV moved to Versailles it gradually became a gathering place for academies and artists. In 1793, during the French Revolution, the Louvre opened as a public museum displaying works of art to the whole nation, symbolizing the change of art from royal private property to national common property. The glass pyramid by I. M. Pei, completed in 1989 as the new main entrance, made this ancient palace a classic example of blending old and new architecture.

stats.label: Glass pyramid
stats.value: Designed by I. M. Pei, opened 1989

stats.label: Pyramid dimensions
stats.value: About 21.6 m high, base about 35 m

stats.label: Annual visitors
stats.value: About 9 million in recent years, the most of any museum in the world

history.text: Before leaving to join the Third Crusade, King Philip II builds the Louvre fortress on the west side of the Paris city wall to defend against enemies.
Charles V converts the fortress into a comfortable royal residence and establishes a royal library holding a large collection of manuscripts.
Francis I orders the medieval fortress demolished, and the architect Pierre Lescot rebuilds it as a Renaissance-style palace.
Louis XIV moves the court to Versailles, and the Louvre is turned over to the academies and artists, who hold the regular art exhibition known as the "Salon."
During the French Revolution the Louvre opens under the name "Central Museum of the Arts," for the first time letting the general public view the royal collections free of charge.
Napoleon III completes the north wing connecting to the Tuileries Palace, realizing the "Grand Louvre" plan of successive monarchs; the Tuileries was later burned during the Paris Commune in 1871.
The Mona Lisa is stolen by the Italian worker Peruggia and recovered in Florence two years later, an affair that made the painting famous.

In the "Grand Louvre" project promoted by President Mitterrand, the glass pyramid designed by I. M. Pei is completed and put into use, and the Ministry of Finance, which had occupied the north wing, subsequently moves out.
In October a theft occurs in the Galerie d'Apollon, in which several French royal jewels are stolen, prompting a comprehensive review of the museum's security.

parts.name: Glass pyramid
parts.description: The glass-and-steel pyramid in the center of the Cour Napoléon is the museum's main entrance, leading visitors into the underground hall.

parts.name: Inverted pyramid
parts.description: A glass pyramid hanging upside down in the center of the underground shopping gallery, with a small stone pyramid beneath its tip facing it.

parts.name: Cour Carrée
parts.description: The oldest palace section of the Louvre, enclosed on four sides by buildings from the Renaissance to the classical period.

parts.name: East colonnade
parts.description: A classical facade completed in the 17th century under Louis XIV, expressing solemn symmetrical beauty with paired Corinthian columns.

parts.name: Grande Galerie
parts.description: A long, narrow gallery extending along the Seine, originally a passage connecting the Louvre and the Tuileries Palace and now displaying Italian painting.

parts.name: The three great wings
parts.description: The Denon, Sully and Richelieu wings, each named for a person; the Mona Lisa is in the Denon wing.

parts.name: Medieval fortress remains
parts.description: The underground exhibition area preserves the moat and tower bases of Philip II's fortress, where one can see the Louvre as it first looked.

parts.name: Galerie d'Apollon
parts.description: A sumptuously gilded gallery decorated in the time of Louis XIV, displaying the French royal jewels and regarded as the forerunner of the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.

detail.architecture: Having been expanded over more than eight hundred years, the Louvre shows medieval fortress, Renaissance palace and 19th-century Second Empire style all in its architecture, a living history of French architecture. I. M. Pei used the transparent glass pyramid as the new entrance so as not to obstruct the surrounding historic facades while bringing a great deal of natural light into the underground hall, solving the original problems of confused circulation and insufficient entrances. The proportions of the pyramid took the Egyptian pyramids at Giza as a reference, its simple geometric form contrasting with and echoing the classical palace.
detail.visit: The Louvre is closed every Tuesday and now admits visitors by reserved time slot, so it is advisable to buy tickets in advance on the official website. The collection is vast and hard to see in a day, so one can first identify key works such as the Mona Lisa, the Venus de Milo and the Winged Victory of Samothrace and plan a route.

forbidden-city.name: Hall of Supreme Harmony, Forbidden City
forbidden-city.description: The foremost of the three great halls of the Forbidden City's outer court, popularly called the "Golden Throne Hall," where the emperors of the Ming and Qing held the most solemn ceremonies such as accession, imperial weddings and the New Year audience, and the largest surviving timber-framed hall in China.
facts: Ten beasts are lined up on the roof ridge, the highest-ranking and unique arrangement in Chinese traditional architecture.
It was repeatedly burned down by lightning or fire in the Ming and Qing, and the existing building was rebuilt in the Kangxi era of the Qing.
Part of the Forbidden City's treasures were moved south in the turmoil of war and later reached Taiwan, becoming the foundation of the collection of the National Palace Museum.

detail.overview: The Hall of Supreme Harmony stands on the central axis of the Forbidden City in Beijing and is the foremost of the three great halls of the outer court, popularly called the "Golden Throne Hall." The Forbidden City was ordered built by the Yongle Emperor of the Ming, who, after seizing the throne through the Jingnan Campaign, decided to move the capital from Nanjing to Beijing, his original fief, in order to strengthen the northern frontier defenses. The Hall of Supreme Harmony was where the emperor held major ceremonies such as accession, imperial weddings, the investiture of empresses, the great New Year and winter solstice audiences, and the sending of generals to war, symbolizing supreme imperial authority. It was repeatedly destroyed by lightning fires and rebuilt, and the existing building dates from the Kangxi era of the Qing, the largest and highest-ranking timber hall surviving in China.

stats.label: Existing building
stats.value: Rebuilt 1695–1697 in the Kangxi era of the Qing

stats.label: Height
stats.value: About 26.9 m (about 35 m including the platform)

stats.label: Roof form
stats.value: Double-eaved hip roof (wudian, the highest rank in ancient architecture)

stats.label: World Heritage Site
stats.value: 1987 (Imperial Palaces of the Ming and Qing Dynasties)

history.text: The Yongle Emperor issues an edict to build the palaces of Beijing, drawing craftsmen, timber and stone from across the country, with more than ten years of preparation and construction in all.
The Forbidden City is completed, its main hall called the "Hall of Worshiping Heaven" (Fengtian Hall); the following year the Ming dynasty formally moves its capital to Beijing.
Only a few months after completion, the three great halls including the Fengtian Hall burn down after being struck by lightning, and are later rebuilt.
The three great halls burn down again in 1557; after reconstruction the Fengtian Hall is renamed the "Huangji Hall."
After the Qing army enters the Pass, the Shunzhi Emperor renames the Huangji Hall the "Taihe Hall" (Hall of Supreme Harmony), meaning the harmony of heaven, earth and all things.
The Hall of Supreme Harmony burns down in 1679, and the Kangxi Emperor orders it rebuilt, giving the building seen today.
After the last emperor Puyi abdicated in 1912 and was expelled from the Forbidden City in 1924, the Palace Museum is founded on October 10 and the palaces open to the public.

Because of the Japanese invasion of China, the Palace Museum's artifacts are crated and moved south; in the late stage of the Chinese Civil War some of the finest pieces reach Taiwan, becoming the foundation of the collection of the National Palace Museum in Taipei.
The Forbidden City in Beijing is inscribed as a World Heritage Site, and in 2004 it is extended to "Imperial Palaces of the Ming and Qing Dynasties," incorporating the Shenyang Imperial Palace.

parts.name: Three-tiered white marble platform
parts.description: The Halls of Supreme Harmony, Central Harmony and Preserving Harmony all stand on a three-tiered white marble platform about 8 meters high, with over a thousand chi-head drainage spouts beneath the balustrades.

parts.name: Double-eaved hip roof
parts.description: A roof with two tiers of eaves and four slopes, covered with yellow glazed tiles, the highest rank, which only the most important imperial halls could use.

parts.name: Roof ridge beasts
parts.description: At the end of the roof ridge an immortal riding a phoenix leads, followed by 10 beasts including dragons, phoenixes and lions, the largest number in Chinese traditional architecture.

parts.name: Golden dragon throne
parts.description: A gilded, dragon-carved throne on the raised dais in the center of the hall, surrounded by six gilded coiled-dragon pillars decorated with raised gilt lines.

parts.name: Caisson ceiling
parts.description: The coiled-dragon caisson in the ceiling above the throne, in which the dragon holds a silvery-white pearl in its mouth, called the "Xuanyuan Mirror."

parts.name: Sundial and standard measure
parts.description: On the terrace in front of the hall a sundial is placed on the east side and a standard grain measure on the west, symbolizing the emperor's control of the realm's time and of its standard weights and measures.

parts.name: Bronze tortoise and crane
parts.description: The bronze tortoise and crane on the terrace symbolize the permanence of the realm and long life, and incense could be burned inside their bellies.

parts.name: Golden brick floor
parts.description: The floor of the hall is paved with fine square bricks specially made in Suzhou, of dense texture and ringing like metal when tapped, hence called "golden bricks."

detail.architecture: The Hall of Supreme Harmony uses the traditional Chinese post-and-lintel timber frame, with columns, beams and bracket sets supporting the huge roof tier by tier, the members joined by mortise and tenon without iron nails, giving good earthquake resistance. In the Ming dynasty the pillars were originally of precious golden-thread nanmu, but when it was rebuilt under Kangxi, as huge timbers were hard to find, they were mostly replaced with pine pieced together. The number of bays, the roof form and the number of roof beasts all follow a strict hierarchy, and the Hall of Supreme Harmony is at the highest level in every respect, expressing in the language of architecture the idea of "the Son of Heaven at the center."
detail.visit: The Palace Museum in Beijing requires real-name reservations for visits and is closed every Monday (except on public holidays), with a daily cap on admissions. The interior of the Hall of Supreme Harmony is not open to enter, but visitors can see the throne and caisson ceiling from outside the hall doors.

deoksugung.name: Junghwajeon Hall, Deoksugung Palace
deoksugung.description: The main hall of Deoksugung Palace, built by Emperor Gojong, who proclaimed the founding of the Korean Empire, and a witness to the turbulent history of Korea's move toward modernity and its confrontation with the great powers and Japanese aggression.
facts: Originally a two-story building in 1902, it burned down in a great fire in 1904 and was rebuilt in 1906 as a single story.
The stone steps in front of the hall are carved with twin dragons, symbolizing the emperor's status, different from the standards of the Joseon kings' era.
Deoksugung has both traditional timber halls and Western-style buildings such as the stone hall, with East and West styles coexisting.

detail.overview: Junghwajeon is the main hall of Deoksugung Palace in Seoul, used for court audiences and state ceremonies. Deoksugung, originally called Gyeongungung, was at first a residence of the Joseon royal family, became a temporary royal palace for the king after the Imjin War, and in the late 19th century became the main palace of Emperor Gojong. Gojong proclaimed the Korean Empire in 1897, hoping to resist the great powers as an independent imperial state, and Junghwajeon was built against this background, decorated to imperial standards with dragon motifs and the like. But the Korean Empire lasted only a little over ten years under Japan's relentless advance, and Junghwajeon thus became a witness to a tragic turning point in modern Korean history.

stats.label: Commissioned by
stats.value: Emperor Gojong of the Korean Empire (Emperor Gwangmu)

stats.label: Use of the building
stats.value: Main hall, where court audiences, celebrations and diplomatic ceremonies were held

stats.label: Original form
stats.value: Two-story building (changed to a single story when rebuilt)

stats.label: Roof form
stats.value: Hip-and-gable roof, multi-cluster bracket sets (dapo style)

history.text: During the Imjin War the palaces of Seoul are burned, and after Seonjo returns to Hanseong he uses a building that had been the residence of Grand Prince Wolsan as a temporary palace.
Gwanghaegun names the temporary palace "Gyeongungung" and later confines Queen Dowager Inmok there.
After Injo's coup overthrows Gwanghaegun, Injo is enthroned at Gyeongungung and then moves to Changdeokgung, and Gyeongungung is long neglected.
Gojong ends his refuge at the Russian legation and returns to Gyeongungung, and in October of the same year proclaims the name "Korean Empire" and declares himself emperor.
To display the status of an imperial state, the two-story Junghwajeon is built as the main hall.
In 1904 a fire at Gyeongungung burns Junghwajeon and other buildings; because of the nation's weakness, it is rebuilt in 1906 as a single story.
Gojong is forced by Japan to abdicate after sending secret envoys to the Hague Peace Conference to expose Japanese aggression, and the palace is renamed "Deoksugung."
Gojong dies suddenly at Deoksugung, giving rise to various rumors about the cause of death, and national feeling runs high, becoming one of the sparks of the March 1st Independence Movement.
Junghwajeon is designated a Korean Treasure and protected as an important heritage of the Korean Empire's history.

parts.name: Junghwajeon
parts.description: The main hall of Deoksugung, standing on a two-tiered stone platform, with a lofty interior; the core space for state ceremonies.

parts.name: Junghwamun
parts.description: The gate directly in front of Junghwajeon, facing the main hall along the central axis, where galleries on both sides originally enclosed the hall courtyard.

parts.name: Rank stones
parts.description: Stone markers lined along both sides of the courtyard in front of the hall, indicating where civil and military officials stood according to their rank.

parts.name: Throne and Sun, Moon and Five Peaks screen
parts.description: The emperor's throne at the center of the hall, with a screen behind painted with the sun, moon and five mountain peaks, symbolizing royal authority and the order of heaven and earth.

parts.name: Twin-dragon decoration
parts.description: Twin dragons are carved and painted on the central ramp stone of the stone steps in front of the hall and on the ceiling inside, showing that this is the palace of an emperor rather than a king.

parts.name: Daehanmun
parts.description: The present main gate of Deoksugung, in front of which a ceremony of the changing of the guards recreating the Joseon dynasty is held every day.

parts.name: Seokjojeon (stone hall)
parts.description: A Neoclassical stone palace completed in 1910, symbolizing the Korean Empire's pursuit of modernization, now the Daehan Empire History Museum.

parts.name: Jeonggwanheon
parts.description: A pavilion that blends Korean and Western styles, said to be where Gojong once savored coffee and received foreign guests.

detail.architecture: Junghwajeon belongs to traditional Joseon timber palace architecture, with a hip-and-gable roof and multi-cluster bracket sets, that is, bracket sets also placed between the columns, to show the exalted status of the main hall. Details such as the dragon motifs and yellow-toned decoration inside and out are evidence that the Korean Empire raised the standard of its architecture according to imperial ritual. Deoksugung has traditional halls and Western-style buildings such as the stone hall side by side, reflecting the character of an era in which the Korean Empire sought a way out between tradition and modernization.
detail.visit: Deoksugung stands next to Seoul City Hall, is closed on Mondays, has cheap admission and also opens in the evening, when the night views have a special charm. In front of Daehanmun there is a ceremony of the changing of the guards every day, and the stone-wall path outside the palace walls is also a famous walking route.

sydney-opera.name: Sydney Opera House
sydney-opera.description: A performing arts center designed by the Danish architect Jørn Utzon, whose tiers of white shell-shaped roofs resemble sails in the harbor, one of the most representative buildings of the 20th century.
facts: The roofs are covered with about 1.05 million white and cream tiles made in Sweden.
It was originally budgeted at about 7 million Australian dollars and expected to take four years, but ended up costing about 102 million Australian dollars and taking 14 years.
It was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2007, one of the few buildings inscribed while its architect was still living.

detail.overview: The Sydney Opera House stands on Bennelong Point in Sydney Harbour, surrounded by water on three sides and facing the Sydney Harbour Bridge. In the 1950s the government of New South Wales wanted to create a world-class performing arts center for Sydney and held an international design competition, which was won by the then little-known Danish architect Jørn Utzon. The tiered white shell-shaped roofs he designed were extremely hard to realize structurally, and the project went through technical difficulties, soaring costs and political disputes; Utzon resigned and left Australia before completion and never saw the finished opera house with his own eyes. After its completion in 1973 it became a national symbol of Australia and is widely regarded as one of the most outstanding buildings of the 20th century.

stats.label: Highest point
stats.value: The top of the shells is about 67 m above sea level

stats.label: Cost
stats.value: Originally estimated at about 7 million Australian dollars, finally about 102 million

history.text: At the urging of the conductor Eugene Goossens and others, New South Wales Premier Joseph Cahill sets up a committee to plan a national opera house.
The international design competition receives 233 entries, and the 38-year-old Jørn Utzon is selected with a sculptural shell-roof scheme.
Work begins hastily before the design is finalized, with the podium platform built first, and later some of the structure has to be demolished and redone.

The shell roofs are hard to calculate and build, and Utzon finally comes up with the "spherical solution," in which all the shell segments are taken from the surface of a single sphere, allowing standardized precasting.

Utzon clashes with the new state minister for public works over funding and design issues and is forced to resign and leave Australia, and the interior design is completed by a team of Australian architects.
On October 20 the opening is presided over by Queen Elizabeth II of Britain, with the construction period extended from the planned 4 years to 14.
The opera house re-engages Utzon to draw up design principles as a basis for future renovations, and the two sides are finally reconciled.
Inscribed as a World Heritage Site; Utzon dies the following year, never having returned to Sydney to see the opera house with his own eyes.
The largest renovation since its opening is carried out, improving the acoustics and accessibility of the concert hall.

parts.name: Shell roofs
parts.description: Several groups of white shells are stacked like sails or seashells, their surfaces patterned in glossy white and matte cream tiles that change color with the weather and light.

parts.name: Concert Hall
parts.description: The largest performance hall in the opera house, with a grand organ of 10,154 pipes, one of the largest mechanical-action organs in the world.

parts.name: Joan Sutherland Theatre
parts.description: Named for the legendary Australian soprano, the main venue for Opera Australia and the Australian Ballet.

parts.name: Drama Theatre and smaller venues
parts.description: Includes the Drama Theatre, the Playhouse and the Studio and other smaller performance spaces, presenting plays, contemporary performance and experimental works.

parts.name: Utzon Room
parts.description: A multipurpose hall remodeled in 2004 to Utzon's own design, with a large tapestry he designed hanging on its wall, the only interior space in the building entirely from his hand.

parts.name: Podium platform and Monumental Steps
parts.description: A huge podium inspired by Mayan temples, with broad steps leading to the entrances of the performance halls.

parts.name: Glass curtain walls
parts.description: Large glass walls at the openings of the shell roofs, allowing audiences to look out over Sydney Harbour during intermissions.

detail.architecture: The shell roofs of the Sydney Opera House are made of 2,194 precast concrete segments held together by tensioned steel cables and then covered with over a million tiles. Utzon's spherical solution allowed every shell to be made with the same curvature, a key breakthrough in turning a complex form into industrialized production, and also one of the early examples of architecture using computers for structural analysis. The building consists of two parts, a massive podium and light roofs, forming a contrast like "earth and clouds."
detail.visit: The Sydney Opera House holds thousands of performances every year, and even without seeing a show one can join a tour of the building to learn about the architecture and Utzon's story. During the Vivid Sydney light festival, the shell roofs become a giant canvas for projected light.
